# ChatGPT and Claude Memory: Fixing the "Goldfish Memory" Problem

**You told it your name last week. You explained your project twice. And today it's asking you to explain everything again — or worse, it's confidently "remembering" things you never said. Memory is the most misunderstood feature in AI chat. Here's how it actually works, and how to make the goldfish act stop.**

No affiliate links here: neither OpenAI nor Anthropic runs a public affiliate program. Everything below works on the free tiers.

---

## What you'll need

- ChatGPT and/or Claude (free accounts are fine — memory features exist on free tiers, with limits)
- Two minutes in your settings — most memory problems are configuration, not capability

[SCREENSHOT: ChatGPT's Settings → Personalization → Memory panel with the key toggles labeled]

---

## How memory actually works in ChatGPT

Two separate systems that people constantly confuse — understanding the split fixes half of all memory complaints.

**System 1: Saved memories.** Discrete facts ChatGPT stores about you — things you told it explicitly ("Remember that I prefer short answers") or things it decided were worth saving. You can view, edit, and delete each one individually.

**System 2: Reference chat history.** ChatGPT drawing on past conversations to personalize new ones — your tone, recurring topics, ongoing projects. Not a browsable list; it's on or off.

**Where the controls live:** Profile picture → **Settings → Personalization → Memory**. From there you can view and manage saved memories (delete single entries or clear everything), toggle memory off (stops *new* saves; existing entries stay until cleared), and toggle reference chat history. You can also manage memory conversationally: "Remember that..." saves one, "Forget that..." removes one.

**Temporary Chat** neither reads nor writes memories — use it for anything you don't want folded into your long-term profile.

**Free vs. paid:** both tiers get the same two-system memory and controls. Paid plans hold more saved entries before older ones get trimmed, and new memory features arrive there first.

---

## How memory actually works in Claude

Claude's memory story changed in 2026: **Claude now has persistent memory across conversations** — rolled out to all users in March 2026, on by default for Free, Pro, and Max plans.

**How it works:** as you chat, Claude saves what it learns as **topics** — your name, preferences, writing style, project context. You manage them under **Settings → Memory**, where every topic can be read, edited, or deleted. Corrections apply globally: fix your company name once and every future conversation reflects it.

**Three things to know:**

1. **It's per-user and private** — not shared with other users, and off by default for Team and Enterprise organizations (an admin enables it there).
2. **Sensitive topics are excluded by default.** Health, beliefs, and similar subjects stay out unless you turn on the "include sensitive topics" setting. Certain data — government IDs, financial account numbers, criminal history — is never stored, toggle or not.
3. **Projects have their own memory.** Each Claude Project keeps a separate memory and project summary — the right home for work context that shouldn't bleed into general chats.

Since August 2026, the same memory also works across regular chat and Claude Cowork, so context carries between them instead of living in two silos.

[SCREENSHOT: Claude's Settings → Memory page showing the Topics list with edit/delete controls]

---

## Fresh-chat hygiene: when to start a new chat vs. continue

Most "memory problems" are actually *chat-hygiene* problems. The rule:

**Continue the same chat when:** you're working on one evolving task — drafting through revisions, debugging one problem, planning one trip. The conversation *is* the working memory, and it's richer than saved memories.

**Start a fresh chat when:**
- The topic genuinely changed (don't plan a vacation in the thread where you debugged code)
- The conversation is very long and answers are degrading (see next section)
- You want a clean, unbiased take without your history coloring it
- You're testing a prompt and don't want past context polluting the result

**The bridge technique:** when a long chat is dying but the work isn't done, prompt:

> Summarize everything important from this conversation — decisions, key facts, open questions — in a compact brief I can paste into a new chat to continue.

Then start fresh and paste the brief as your first message. You keep the substance and shed the dead weight.

---

## Long-conversation degradation and context resets

Every chat has a context window — a limit on how much conversation the model can consider at once. Near the limit, the oldest parts silently fall out. The model doesn't warn you; it just starts forgetting the beginning while sounding just as confident.

**The symptoms:** contradictions of earlier decisions, re-asking for information you gave, answers getting vaguer as the chat grows.

**The honest complication:** in September–October 2026, users on OpenAI's developer forum reported long chats losing usable context *earlier* than before, and saved memories not being retrieved unless explicitly requested. These are **user-reported issues, not confirmed product bugs** — but consistent enough to plan around.

**What to do about it:**
1. **Watch for symptoms**, not a warning banner — there isn't one.
2. **Summarize-and-restart** once a chat passes ~50–80 messages or answers start degrading.
3. **Test suspected loss directly:** "What did we decide about X in this conversation?" If it can't answer, the context is gone — restart with a summary.
4. **For critical long projects, use Projects** (in both ChatGPT and Claude) instead of one mega-chat. Project memory is built for durable context that survives across individual conversations.

---

## Confabulation recovery: when the model invents your conversation

The nastiest memory failure isn't forgetting — it's *confabulating*: the model confidently "remembers" something from your conversation that never happened. An invented decision, a quote you never said. Framed as memory, it bypasses your skepticism.

**The recovery sequence — correct, restate, restart:**

1. **Correct it explicitly.** "That's not right — I never said that. Here's what I actually said: [the truth]." Uncorrected, a false memory becomes the foundation for everything after.
2. **Restate the real facts.** Follow up with the key true facts in one clean message. If the tool supports saved memories, save the correction: "Remember: [correct fact]."
3. **Restart if it persists.** If the model keeps returning to the invented version, the conversation is contaminated — summarize the *true* state and start fresh. A clean restart beats ten rounds of arguing with a confused context window.

**Prevention:** for facts that must survive across chats, save them explicitly ("Remember that...") and verify with "What do you remember about X?" before building on them.

[SCREENSHOT: A chat showing the correct → restate → restart sequence after a confabulated memory]

---

## Saving key facts with memory entries

Ambient memory (what the model saves on its own) is unreliable by design — it guesses what's worth keeping. Explicit memory entries are the reliable layer. Build the habit:

- **After any important decision:** "Remember: we're launching in March, budget is $5k, audience is first-time founders."
- **For standing preferences:** "Remember that I want code examples in Python, with comments explaining each step."
- **For projects:** "Remember that Project Atlas is the Q1 website redesign, not the mobile app."
- **Audit monthly:** open your memory list, delete the stale (old jobs, finished trips), correct the wrong. Memory rots — five minutes a month keeps it trustworthy.

**What not to save:** passwords, financial account numbers, ID numbers, or anything you wouldn't want on a company's servers. Claude refuses some of this automatically; ChatGPT won't stop you, so stop yourself. Use Temporary Chat for anything sensitive.

---

## Common mistakes table

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Expecting memory to work like a human brain | Surprise when it forgets or misremembers | Treat it as a filing cabinet: useful, fallible, needs curation |
| Never opening memory settings | Stale/wrong facts silently shaping answers | Monthly audit: view, correct, delete |
| One mega-chat for everything | Degradation, contradictions, lost context | Fresh chats per topic; summarize-and-restart past ~50–80 messages |
| Relying on auto-saved memory | Key facts never saved; trivia saved instead | Save key facts explicitly with "Remember that..." |
| Letting confabulation stand | Invented "memories" derailing the chat | Correct → restate → restart |
| Sensitive data in memory | Private info stored on company servers | Temporary Chat for sensitive topics; never save IDs/passwords/finances |
| Outdated Claude knowledge | "Claude has no memory" (wrong since March 2026) | Check Settings → Memory |

---

## Before/after checklist

Run through this when memory misbehaves:- [ ] Checked what's actually stored? (ChatGPT: "What do you remember about me?" / Claude: Settings → Memory → Topics)
- [ ] Is the fact I expect actually saved — or did I just assume?
- [ ] Right chat, or time for a fresh one? (topic changed? chat very long?)
- [ ] Long chat degrading: summarize-and-restart instead of pushing through
- [ ] Model invented our history: correct, restate, restart if it persists
- [ ] Cross-chat facts saved explicitly, not just mentioned once
- [ ] Sensitive info in Temporary Chat, never in memory

---

## Pricing note (USD, as of October 2026)

Memory features are available on the free tiers of both tools, with limits. You don't need to pay to fix goldfish memory.| Plan | Price | What matters for memory |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT Free | $0 | Saved memories + chat-history reference included; smaller memory budget |
| ChatGPT Plus | $20/mo | Larger memory capacity; new memory features arrive here first |
| Claude Free | $0 | Persistent memory on by default; Topics view/edit/delete included |
| Claude Pro | $20/mo (or ~$17/mo billed annually) | Same memory features; higher usage limits overall |

**When to upgrade:** for usage limits and stronger models, not for memory — the controls are identical on free. Paid buys capacity (more entries before old ones get trimmed), which only matters for heavy users.

*Prices change — confirm at the providers' official pricing pages before you buy.*

---

## FAQ

**Why does ChatGPT forget things I told it last week?**
Three usual causes: the fact was never saved as a memory (mentioning isn't saving — use "Remember that..."), an old entry got trimmed when the memory budget filled, or you're hitting the retrieval issues users reported in Sept–Oct 2026 (ask explicitly: "check your memory for X"). Check what's stored before assuming it's broken.

**Is Claude's memory really on by default? I thought Claude didn't have memory.**
It didn't, until March 2026 — that's where the confusion comes from. Persistent memory rolled out to all Claude users in March 2026 and is on by default for Free, Pro, and Max. Check Settings → Memory to see your Topics.

**Should I turn memory off for privacy?**
Your call. You can disable memory and chat-history reference in ChatGPT's Personalization settings, or pause memory in Claude's Memory settings — and use Temporary Chat (ChatGPT) for anything you want kept out entirely. Either way, don't store sensitive personal data in memory.

**What's the difference between Projects and memory?**
Memory is global context about *you* that follows you across chats. Projects are scoped workspaces — each has its own files, instructions, and memory, ideal for ongoing work (a book draft, a codebase) that shouldn't mix with general chats. Use Projects for work; memory for personal context.

**The model insists it remembers something I never said. What now?**
Correct it once, restate the truth, and if it keeps returning to the invented version, restart with a clean summary. Don't debate a contaminated context window — replace it.

# ComfyUI and Stable Diffusion: From Broken Workflows to Your First Good Image

**You downloaded a workflow from the internet, loaded it, and the screen turned into a crime scene of red error boxes. Everybody's first hour with ComfyUI looks like this. Here's the order of operations that gets you from red boxes to a real image.**

ComfyUI is free, open-source, and absurdly powerful — and its error messages assume you've already read the source code. This tutorial covers the five failures every beginner hits, in the order you'll hit them: installing the wrong build, missing nodes, VRAM errors, bad hands and text, and finally a minimal workflow that just works.

---

## What you'll need

- A computer with a dedicated GPU — **8GB+ of VRAM** is the comfortable minimum for standard models; 6GB can work with the VRAM tricks in Step 3
- **10–15GB of free disk space** (ComfyUI itself is small; the checkpoint model files are not)
- One checkpoint model file (`.safetensors`) — for example, any Stable Diffusion 1.5 or SDXL checkpoint from a reputable source. Place it in `ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/`
- Patience for one restart. There is always one restart.

[SCREENSHOT: A fresh ComfyUI install showing the default empty workflow canvas in the browser]

---

## Step 1: Install the right build (pick one, not all three)

There are three legitimate ways to install ComfyUI. They run the same engine — the difference is who manages the Python environment.

| Build | Best for | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **ComfyUI Desktop app** (from comfy.org/download) | First-time users | One-click install with auto-updates, but you don't control the underlying Python environment |
| **Windows portable `.7z`** | Full control without installing Python | Extract with 7-Zip, double-click `run_nvidia_gpu.bat`. Bundled PyTorch is fixed; updating means re-downloading |
| **Stability Matrix** | Several tools side by side | One-click package manager with a shared model library so checkpoints aren't duplicated |

**Recommendation:** start with the **Desktop app** if you just want images today, or **Stability Matrix** if you'll try multiple interfaces. The portable build is the power-user path — full control, full responsibility.

**What about the classic WebUI?** If node graphs feel like overkill, the maintained path in 2026 is **Forge Neo** (the `sd-webui-forge-classic` repo's Neo branch) — a community-maintained continuation of lllyasviel's Stable Diffusion WebUI Forge, which went quiet when its author got busy. It's the familiar AUTOMATIC1111-style interface with better memory handling, and Stability Matrix can install it too. Everything below still applies to ComfyUI specifically, which is where the serious control lives.

[SCREENSHOT: Stability Matrix package list showing ComfyUI and Forge as installable packages]

---

## Step 2: Fix missing-node errors (the red boxes)

**What you're seeing:** nodes outlined in red with errors like "node type not found." This is not corruption — it means the workflow was built with **custom nodes** (community plugins) that aren't installed in your ComfyUI.

**The fix, in order:**

1. **Use the Manager.** Install **ComfyUI Manager** if you don't have it (it's the standard node/plugin manager — most installs include it). In the Manager menu, click **"Install Missing Custom Nodes."** It scans the loaded workflow, lists the node packs it needs, and installs them. Then **restart ComfyUI completely** — nodes only load at startup.
2. **If a node still fails to load**, check the terminal/console window ComfyUI launched from. A `ModuleNotFoundError` means a Python dependency is missing. Install it with the *same* Python that runs ComfyUI — for the portable build that's:
   ```
   python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install -r ComfyUI\custom_nodes\<node-folder>\requirements.txt
   ```
   Then restart again.
3. **If ComfyUI won't start at all after installing nodes**, launch with `--disable-all-custom-nodes`. If it boots, a custom node is the culprit — re-enable them in halves until you find the bad one. Keep your models and workflows in folders separate from the ComfyUI install, so nuking and reinstalling the app never costs you your library.

**Prevention:** check whether a workflow's author lists required custom nodes, and install them *before* loading the workflow.

[SCREENSHOT: ComfyUI Manager menu with "Install Missing Custom Nodes" highlighted, and a workflow with red missing nodes]

---

## Step 3: Fix VRAM errors (the out-of-memory ladder)

**What you're seeing:** `CUDA out of memory` in red text. Your GPU ran out of video memory mid-generation. Work this ladder from top to bottom — stop at the first rung that works:

1. **Lower the resolution and batch size.** A 512×512 single image uses a fraction of the memory of a 1024×1024 batch of four. Get it working small first.
2. **Use a quantized model.** FP8 versions of checkpoints (or GGUF variants) load the same model at roughly half the memory. If your model ships an FP8 variant, try it — the quality difference is small on most models.
3. **Enable tiled VAE decode.** Decoding the image in tiles instead of all at once trades speed for memory. Slower, but it gets big images through small cards.
4. **Add `--lowvram` to your launch flags.** This makes ComfyUI shuffle models between VRAM and system RAM instead of keeping everything loaded. It's slower (more loading between stages) but dramatically lowers peak VRAM.
5. **Escalate if needed:** `--novram` with `--cache-none` offloads even more aggressively, and `--reserve-vram` leaves a safety margin so the run doesn't fail at peak usage.

**Two things people get wrong:**

- `--medvram` **does not exist in ComfyUI.** It's an AUTOMATIC1111 flag that tutorials keep copy-pasting. Using it does nothing — or errors.
- `--normalvram` forces the default memory mode. You generally don't need it; it's there to *undo* the other flags if a previous guide left them in your launch command.

*AMD note: on AMD cards under Windows, the portable build runs through DirectML, which limits some optimizations (community reports FP8 issues there). AMD users should check ComfyUI's current docs for the recommended backend before assuming the VRAM ladder above applies one-to-one.* [Partially verified — treat AMD specifics as "check current docs."]

[SCREENSHOT: ComfyUI launch options / .bat file showing --lowvram added to the startup flags]

---

## Step 4: Fix the classic hand and text problems

**Why it happens:** hands are anatomically complex, and in training data they usually appear small, in motion, or partially hidden — the model rarely sees a crisp close-up of six fingers... er, five fingers. Text fails for a similar reason: the model learned what text *looks like* (shapes on signs) without learning to spell. Both problems get worse at low resolution, where there aren't enough pixels to render fine detail.

**The fixes, cheapest first:**

1. **Negative prompt.** Add to the negative prompt field: `bad hands, deformed hands, extra fingers, mutated hands, poorly drawn hands, blurry text, gibberish text, watermark`. This alone fixes a surprising number of cases.
2. **Generate bigger — or upscale after.** Hands drawn at 512px are blobs; the same hands at 1024px have room for fingers. Either generate at higher resolution directly or generate small and run a second **hires-fix / upscale pass**, which re-renders details at higher fidelity.
3. **Inpaint the problem area.** Mask just the bad hand (or the garbled sign), keep everything else frozen, and regenerate only the masked region with a focused prompt like `detailed human hand, five fingers, natural pose`. Targeted repair beats rerolling the whole image.
4. **Use a detailer node.** Community packs (e.g. the Impact Pack's FaceDetailer) automate the detect-and-repair loop: find, crop, enhance, blend back. Install via the Manager like any other custom node (Step 2).

[SCREENSHOT: Before/after — a six-fingered hand vs. the same image after inpainting repair]

---

## Step 5: A minimal working text-to-image workflow

Forget downloaded workflows for a moment. Build this from scratch once and you'll understand every workflow you'll ever load. Seven nodes:

```
[Checkpoint Loader] → model ──→ [KSampler]
     ├─ clip ──→ [CLIP Text Encode: positive prompt] ──→ positive ──→ [KSampler]
     ├─ clip ──→ [CLIP Text Encode: negative prompt] ──→ negative ──→ [KSampler]
     └─ vae ───→ [VAE Decode] ←──────── samples ── [KSampler]
[Empty Latent Image] ──→ latent ──→ [KSampler]
[VAE Decode] ──→ image ──→ [Save Image]
```

**What each node does, in plain language:**

| Node | Job |
|---|---|
| Checkpoint Loader | Loads your `.safetensors`; outputs model, clip (text understanding), vae (image encoding) |
| CLIP Text Encode ×2 | Turns your prompt and your "avoid this" list into model-readable numbers |
| Empty Latent Image | The blank canvas — **512×512** to start |
| KSampler | The actual generation: runs the denoising loop |
| VAE Decode | Converts the result into a viewable image |
| Save Image | Writes the PNG to your output folder |

**Sane starting settings on the KSampler:** seed = any (use "randomize" while exploring, fix it when iterating), steps = 20–25, CFG = 7, sampler = `euler`, scheduler = `normal`, denoise = 1.0.

**Your first prompt:** positive `a cozy cabin in a snowy forest at dusk, warm light in windows, cinematic` — negative `blurry, deformed, watermark, text`. Queue it. If you get an image, everything works and every future problem is a *workflow* problem, not an *installation* problem — which is a much better place to be.

[SCREENSHOT: The complete seven-node workflow wired up, with the first generated cabin image in the Save Image preview]

---

## Common mistakes table

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Loading a downloaded workflow first | Red missing-node boxes everywhere | Install via Manager → "Install Missing Custom Nodes," then restart |
| Installing nodes but not restarting | Nodes still red after install | Custom nodes load at startup — restart ComfyUI completely |
| Generating 1024×1024 on a 6GB card | `CUDA out of memory` | Start at 512×512; climb the VRAM ladder (Step 3) |
| Using `--medvram` | Nothing happens (or an error) | It doesn't exist in ComfyUI — use `--lowvram` instead |
| No negative prompt | Deformed hands, stray text, watermarks | Add a proper negative prompt (Step 4) |
| Rerolling whole images for one bad hand | Wasted generations | Inpaint the masked region; use a detailer node |
| Mixing Python environments | `ModuleNotFoundError` persists after pip install | Use the *same* Python that launches ComfyUI (portable: `python_embeded\python.exe`) |
| Nuking the ComfyUI folder to "fix" it | Models and workflows gone | Keep models/workflows outside the install folder; reinstall the app, not the library |

---

## First-image checklist

- [ ] ComfyUI launches and opens at `http://127.0.0.1:8188` (or your configured port)
- [ ] One checkpoint model sits in `models/checkpoints/` and appears in the loader dropdown
- [ ] ComfyUI Manager is installed
- [ ] The seven-node workflow is wired: checkpoint → encoders → latent → sampler → decode → save
- [ ] KSampler at 512×512, 20 steps, CFG 7, euler
- [ ] Negative prompt includes hand/text quality terms
- [ ] First image generates without red errors — quality comes later, *working* comes first

---

## Pricing note (USD, as of October 2026)

**ComfyUI and Stable Diffusion are free and open-source.** No subscription, no account, no credits — the software costs $0, and it runs offline after setup. Your costs are hardware and electricity.

**Optional: cloud GPU rental** (if your local GPU can't keep up). Approximate on-demand rates, which fluctuate:

| GPU | VRAM | ≈ Price/hr |
|---|---|---|
| RTX 3090 | 24 GB | ~$0.22–0.50 |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | ~$0.34–0.74 |
| A100 80GB | 80 GB | ~$1.19–1.59 |

*Approximate — community vs. secure tiers differ, and prices move. Check the provider's live pricing before budgeting.* Providers like RunPod ship ready-made ComfyUI templates, so you can rent a pod, generate, download results, and terminate — paying only for the hours you use. Stopped-but-not-terminated machines can still incur storage charges, so terminate when you're done.

*Neither ComfyUI nor Stable Diffusion operates a public affiliate program we could verify, so this tutorial carries no affiliate links.*

---

## FAQ

**Which install method should a total beginner pick?**
The Desktop app from comfy.org — one-click install with auto-updates. Move to the portable build or Stability Matrix when you start installing lots of custom nodes or want multiple UIs.

**I installed the missing nodes and they're still red. Why?**
You didn't restart ComfyUI (nodes load at startup), or a Python dependency failed to install — check the console for `ModuleNotFoundError` and install it with the same Python that launches ComfyUI.

**How much VRAM do I actually need?**
8GB is comfortable for SD 1.5/SDXL-class models at moderate resolutions. 6GB works with `--lowvram` and FP8 models. Below that, consider cloud GPU rental rather than fighting your hardware.

**Why are the hands still bad with a negative prompt?**
The negative prompt reduces the frequency; it doesn't rewrite anatomy. For a keeper image, inpaint the hand region with a focused prompt, or run a detailer node over it. Some seeds are just cursed — change the seed.

**Can I use ComfyUI commercially?**
ComfyUI itself is open-source, but **check the license of each checkpoint model** — many community models carry their own use restrictions. The tool being free doesn't make every model free for commercial work.

**Do I need the internet to use ComfyUI?**
No — after installation and model download, it runs fully offline. That's one of its biggest advantages over cloud services.

title: n8n AI Agents: Your First Working Automation Without the Loop-from-Hell
description: Your agent called the same tool 47 times, drained your OpenAI balance, and answered nothing. Here's how to build your first working n8n AI agent — and the one setting that stops it from looping forever.
content:
# n8n AI Agents: Your First Working Automation Without the Loop-from-Hell

**Your agent called the same tool 47 times, drained your OpenAI balance, and answered nothing. Here's how to build your first working n8n AI agent — and the one setting that stops it from looping forever.**

---

## What you'll need

- **n8n** — self-hosted (free) or an n8n Cloud trial; either works for this tutorial
- **An LLM API key** from any supported provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) — you pay the model provider separately from n8n
- **One concrete task** for your agent, narrow enough to describe in a sentence (e.g. "triage incoming support emails into urgent / normal / spam")

n8n is a workflow automation platform with a visual canvas: you connect nodes (triggers, apps, AI models) into workflows that run automatically. The **AI Agent node** is what turns a workflow into an agent — it can reason, call tools, and decide its own next step instead of following a fixed path.

[SCREENSHOT: n8n canvas showing Chat Trigger → AI Agent → Chat Model nodes connected]

---

## Step 1: Build the minimum viable agent (four nodes)

A working n8n agent needs just four pieces:

1. **Chat Trigger node** — gives you a chat window to talk to the agent while you build and test.
2. **AI Agent node** — the brain. Connect the Chat Trigger to it.
3. **Chat Model node** — attach this to the agent's model input and paste in your API key. This is the LLM the agent thinks with.
4. **An output** — the agent's answer flows out of the AI Agent node to whatever comes next (a Chat Response node, a Slack message, a spreadsheet row — anything).

Open the AI Agent node and write a **system prompt** with three ingredients:

- **Role + scope:** what the agent is and what it's allowed to touch. *"You are a support-email triage agent. You read incoming emails and classify them. You do not reply to anyone."*
- **An exit path:** *"If you cannot complete the task with the tools available, summarize what you found and stop. Never invent data."*
- **No guessing:** this one sentence prevents an entire class of failures — models will confidently fabricate order details or policy specifics unless told otherwise.

[SCREENSHOT: AI Agent node settings panel with the system prompt field and Max Iterations field highlighted]

**Activate the workflow, type a test message in the chat, and watch the agent work.** If it answers correctly on the first try — congratulations, you have a working agent. Now make it production-proof.

---

## Step 2: Defeat the loop-from-hell (set Max Iterations)

Here's the failure that eats every beginner: the **loop-from-hell**. The agent calls the same tool with slightly different arguments — twelve times, twenty times, fifty times — then either fails with a generic error or produces a rambling answer. Your LLM bill spikes on a single bad input.

Why it happens is structural: **an agent stops only when the model *decides* it's done.** On confusing inputs, the model doesn't decide — it keeps gathering "one more" piece of context. Vague tool descriptions and too many tools make it worse: if a human couldn't decide which tool to call, the agent can't either.

Three defenses, in order of importance:

### 1. Set Max Iterations on the AI Agent node

This is the single most important setting in this tutorial. Find **Max Iterations** in the agent node's options and set it:

- **5–8** for most agents (a sensible production default)
- **Up to 25** for research workflows that genuinely need many reasoning steps

One honest caveat: Max Iterations is a cliff, not a guardrail. When the cap is hit, the execution usually fails with a generic error — no partial result, no summary of what burned. That's why it's defense #1 of three, not the only one.

### 2. Give the agent an escape hatch in the system prompt

Add this line to every agent prompt: *"If you cannot complete the task within your available steps, summarize what you found so far and stop."* This gives the model a graceful failure path — a summary instead of a 50-call spiral.

### 3. Attach the minimal viable toolset

Only connect the tools this agent actually needs. For each tool, write a clear description: **what it does, what input it expects, what it returns.** The agent picks tools based on those descriptions, so a vague description ("does stuff with data") is a direct cause of loops.

[SCREENSHOT: AI Agent node with two clearly-described tools attached vs. a cluttered agent with twelve vague tools]

---

## Step 3: Add error handling before you need it

Agents are nondeterministic — they behave like a slow, expensive external API with unpredictable latency and cost. Production workflows need budgets and fallbacks around them:

- **Wire error outputs on fallible nodes.** Every node that can fail (HTTP requests, database writes, third-party APIs) has an error output. Connect it to a fallback: a notification, a logged error row, or a safe default — not silence.
- **Turn on retry for flaky APIs.** For network nodes, enable retry-on-fail with a small number of attempts (3 is typical) and a wait between tries. Transient failures shouldn't kill the workflow.
- **Create an Error Trigger workflow.** This is a separate n8n workflow that automatically catches failures from your other workflows. Have it notify you on a channel you actually read. One rule: don't let the error workflow's own failure notify through the same channel — that's a recursion trap.
- **Set explicit limits around the agent.** Timeouts where available, a cap on tool calls per execution, and a fallback route: if the agent times out, returns invalid output, or exceeds budget, the workflow should do something deliberate — send to human review, ask the user for clarification, or use a deterministic fallback.

---

## Step 4: Debug with execution logs

When something goes wrong, n8n's execution log is your crime scene. Open the failed execution and walk through it node by node:

1. **See what the agent actually did.** Enable intermediate-steps output on the agent node to watch its tool-call reasoning — which tools it called, with what arguments, and what came back. Most loops are obvious the moment you can see them.
2. **Re-run with pinned data.** Re-run the failing execution a few times with the same input. If the output changes between runs, your agent is non-deterministic — **lower the temperature** on the model node to 0.1–0.3 for factual work. (Higher temperatures are for creative tasks; support agents that improvise are a liability.)
3. **Add checkpoints so errors stop early.** A Structured Output Parser makes bad formats fail immediately instead of poisoning downstream steps. An IF node between steps can validate key fields before the workflow continues.
4. **Keep memory short.** Don't let long chat history be the agent's source of truth — stale data entered at turn 2 quietly corrupts every answer after it. Re-fetch important facts from your database when the agent needs them.

[SCREENSHOT: execution log view showing node-by-node status and the agent's intermediate steps]

---

## Common mistakes table

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Max Iterations left unset | Agent loops 20–50 tool calls, LLM bill spikes, execution dies with a generic error | Set 5–8 (25 for research); add an exit instruction to the prompt |
| Twelve vague tools attached | Agent calls the wrong tool or loops between similar ones | Attach only needed tools; write precise descriptions (what, input, output) |
| No exit path in the system prompt | Model never "decides" it's done | "If you can't complete it, summarize and stop" |
| Temperature 0.7+ on a factual agent | Same input, different output every run | 0.1–0.3 for factual/support work |
| No error branch on API nodes | One 400 error kills the workflow silently | Wire each fallible node's error output to a fallback |
| Long chat memory as source of truth | A wrong fact at turn 2 corrupts everything after | Keep memory short; re-fetch facts from the database |
| Testing only on perfect inputs | Loop-from-hell appears the first time real data arrives | Test with messy, ambiguous, and adversarial inputs |

---

## Before-you-ship checklist

Run through this before any agent touches real data:

- [ ] Max Iterations set (5–8 typical, 25 for research)
- [ ] System prompt has a role, a scope, and an exit path
- [ ] Only the necessary tools are attached, each with a clear description
- [ ] Temperature at 0.1–0.3 for factual work
- [ ] Error outputs wired on every fallible node
- [ ] An Error Trigger workflow exists and notifies a channel you read
- [ ] You know the cost of one execution (n8n execution + your model provider's tokens)
- [ ] Tested with pinned data, multiple runs, ambiguous inputs

---

## Pricing note (USD, as of October 2026)

n8n meters **executions** — one full workflow run counts as one execution, no matter how many nodes are inside it.

| Plan | Price | Executions/mo | What matters for agents |
|---|---|---|---|
| Community (self-hosted) | $0 | Unlimited | Free software; you pay only for the server (~$5–7/mo on a small VPS) |
| Starter (Cloud) | $24/mo ($20/mo annual) | 2,500 | Cheapest managed option; fine for learning and light use |
| Pro (Cloud) | $60/mo ($50/mo annual) | 10,000 | Workflow history, variables, higher concurrency |
| Business / Enterprise | Custom | Custom | SSO, audit logs, SLAs |

**Two things beginners miss:** (1) your LLM costs are *separate* — they go to your model provider, not n8n, and a looping agent burns both meters at once; (2) when you hit a Cloud execution cap, workflows stop until the cycle resets — there are no automatic overages. Start self-hosted or on Starter while learning, and cost one typical execution before scaling up.

*Prices change — confirm on n8n's pricing page before you buy.*

---

## FAQ

**Why did my agent run for minutes and then fail with a generic error?**
It almost certainly hit Max Iterations or n8n's maximum execution time — the loop-from-hell. Open the execution log, check the agent's intermediate steps to see the loop, then tighten Max Iterations, prune the toolset, and add an exit instruction to the prompt.

**Can I really run n8n free forever?**
Yes — the self-hosted Community Edition is free with unlimited executions. The only cost is the server it runs on, typically a few dollars a month for a small VPS.

**Do AI agent workflows cost extra on n8n Cloud?**
No separate AI tier exists — agents run on the same execution model. But one execution can trigger many LLM calls, so budget your model provider's token costs separately.

**What's a good first agent project?**
Something with a narrow toolset and a clear success signal: an email triage bot, a meeting-notes summarizer, or a FAQ bot over your own docs. Avoid multi-agent setups until one agent is boring and reliable.

**Should I use an agent at all, or just a regular workflow?**
If the task has fixed steps, use a regular workflow — it's cheaper, faster, and deterministic. Reach for the agent node only when the path genuinely depends on judgment (classifying, researching, deciding which tool fits).

---

title: Ollama and Local LLMs: Run AI Free Without the Setup Nightmare
description: The computer on your desk can already run a capable AI assistant — no subscription, no account, no data leaving your machine. Here's the full setup in under 30 minutes, including a ChatGPT-style interface.
content:
# Ollama and Local LLMs: Run AI Free Without the Setup Nightmare

**The computer on your desk can already run a capable AI assistant — no subscription, no account, no data leaving your machine. Here's the full setup in under 30 minutes, including a ChatGPT-style interface.**

---

## What you'll need

- A computer with **8GB+ RAM** (16GB is comfortable) and ~10GB of free disk space
- Internet access for the one-time download — after that, everything works **offline**
- Optional: Docker, if you want the pretty chat interface (Step 4)

Ollama is a free, open-source tool that downloads and runs large language models directly on your machine. No cloud account, no per-message fees, no one reading your prompts. The catch — and it's the only real one — is that your hardware decides how smart and how fast your local AI can be.

[SCREENSHOT: terminal showing `ollama run qwen3:8b` with the model's first response streaming in]

---

## Step 1: Install Ollama (one command)

Pick your operating system and paste one command into a terminal:

- **macOS / Linux:**
  ```
  curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
  ```
- **Windows:** download the installer from Ollama's website, or in PowerShell:
  ```
  irm https://ollama.com/install.ps1 | iex
  ```

Verify it worked:

```
ollama --version
```

That's the entire installation. Ollama runs as a background server on your machine (at `localhost:11434`), and everything else is just telling it which model to load.

[SCREENSHOT: terminal showing the install command and the version check succeeding]

---

## Step 2: Pull your first model

Models are downloaded with `ollama pull` and started with `ollama run`. Here are the beginner-safe picks, based on 2026 community guides:

**The recommended first pull:**

```
ollama pull qwen3:8b
ollama run qwen3:8b
```

Qwen3 8B is the strongest all-rounder in its size class right now — good at chat, writing, coding, and reasoning — and it runs comfortably on a machine with 8–12GB of available memory. Type a question, hit enter, and you're chatting with an AI that lives entirely on your hardware.

**Alternatives worth knowing:**

| Situation | Command | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Solid general alternative | `ollama run llama3.1:8b` | Meta's workhorse — reliable chat and instruction-following |
| Weak hardware or maximum speed | `ollama run llama3.2:3b` | Runs on ~8GB RAM; fine for summaries and drafting |
| Even smaller / older laptop | `ollama run phi3` or `ollama run mistral` | Tiny and fast when nothing else fits |
| Coding focus | `ollama run qwen2.5-coder:7b` | Fine-tuned for code; noticeably better at programming than general models |

**Useful commands to remember:**

```
ollama list    # show installed models
ollama pull <name>   # download a model
ollama run <name>    # chat with a model
ollama rm <name>     # delete a model to free disk space
```

> Model names move fast — new versions land every few months. If a tag above ever fails, check the current model library on Ollama's website for the latest names.

[SCREENSHOT: `ollama list` showing two downloaded models with their sizes]

---

## Step 3: Size the model to your hardware (approximate guide)

This is where beginners waste an afternoon: downloading a 70-billion-parameter model onto a laptop and watching it crawl. The rule is simple — **match the model to your free memory, not your ambition.**

These are approximate figures for the default quantization Ollama ships with (a good size/quality trade-off). Treat them as guidelines, not guarantees:

| Your free memory | Comfortable range | Example picks |
|---|---|---|
| 4–6 GB | 1B–3B models | `llama3.2:1b`, `phi3` |
| 8 GB | 3B–8B models | `llama3.2:3b`, `qwen3:8b`, `mistral` |
| 16 GB | 8B–14B models | `qwen3:8b`, `phi4`, `deepseek-r1:14b` |

1. **If it runs but crawls, it's spilling to disk.** The model doesn't fit in memory and your machine is swapping — drop down one size and it'll feel 10x faster.

  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \

  --name open-webui \

1. Open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser.
2. Create an account — **the first user to register automatically becomes the admin.**
3. Open WebUI auto-detects your local Ollama and lists your downloaded models in the dropdown. Pick one and start chatting.

| Use case | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday chat, writing, summarizing | `qwen3:8b` or `llama3.1:8b` | Best quality per gigabyte; the 2026 sweet spot |
| Coding and code review | `qwen2.5-coder:7b` (small) / `qwen3-coder:30b` (32GB+) | Fine-tuned for programming; beats general models of the same size on code |
| Hard reasoning, math, multi-step problems | `deepseek-r1:14b` (16GB+) or `gpt-oss:20b` | Reasoning-focused models that "think step by step" — slower, but stronger on hard questions |

Switching is free and instant — `ollama run <other-model>` or the dropdown in Open WebUI. Download a few, keep the ones you actually use, delete the rest with `ollama rm`.

---

## When local beats cloud (and when it doesn't)

**Local wins on three things, decisively:**

- **Privacy.** Your prompts never leave your machine. No account required for basic Ollama use. For sensitive documents, journal entries, or client work, this alone is the reason.
- **Cost.** $0 marginal cost per message. Ask it 500 questions a day — the bill doesn't move.
- **Offline.** Once models are downloaded, no internet needed. Planes, dead zones, and outages don't matter.

**Cloud still wins on two things:**

- **Frontier capability.** The biggest cloud models still beat anything that fits on a laptop for the hardest reasoning, complex coding, and cutting-edge multimodal work. Local 8B models are genuinely good now — but they're not frontier.
- **Zero maintenance.** Local means you manage disk space, updates, and model choices. Cloud means someone else does.

The honest setup for most people: **local for everyday work and anything private, cloud for the 5% of tasks that need frontier power.** That combination deletes most subscription bills without deleting capability.

## Common mistakes table

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Downloading a 70B model on 8GB RAM | Generation crawls at 1 token/second or crashes | Match model size to free memory (Step 3); start with a 3B–8B model |
| Skipping the version check | Terminal says `command not found` later | Run `ollama --version` right after install |
| Forgetting Ollama must be running | Open WebUI shows no models | Start Ollama first — the UI is just a frontend |
| Using one model for everything | Mediocre code from a chat model | Keep a chat model + a coder model; switch freely |
| Never deleting models | Disk fills up silently (models are GBs each) | `ollama list` regularly; `ollama rm` what you don't use |
| Expecting frontier-level reasoning from 3B | Wrong answers on hard problems | Small models draft and summarize; reach for 14B+ or cloud for hard reasoning |
| Pasting secrets into a cloud chatbot instead | Unnecessary data exposure | If it's sensitive, run it locally — that's the whole point |

---

## Setup checklist

- [ ] Ollama installed and `ollama --version` returns a version
- [ ] First model pulled and chatting (`ollama run qwen3:8b`)
- [ ] Model size fits your free memory — no disk-spill crawling
- [ ] Open WebUI running at `http://localhost:3000` (optional but recommended)
- [ ] Admin account created; models auto-detected in the dropdown
- [ ] A coding model installed if you write code
- [ ] Old/unused models removed with `ollama rm`

---

## Pricing note (USD, as of October 2026)

Ollama is **free and open-source**. Open WebUI is **free and open-source**. The models are **free to download**. There is no subscription, no credit system, and no per-message cost — the hardware you already own is the entire price of admission.

The only money involved is optional: a machine with more RAM (or a GPU) runs bigger, smarter models. But the setup in this tutorial — a capable 8B assistant with a polished chat interface — costs exactly **$0** on any reasonably modern computer.

---

## FAQ

**Will this replace my ChatGPT subscription?**
For everyday chat, writing, summarizing, and private documents — yes, for most people. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, keep a cloud option for the 5% of questions that need frontier models.

**Do I need a GPU?**
No. An NVIDIA GPU or Apple Silicon makes generation noticeably faster, but Ollama runs on CPU too — just slower. A 3B model on an ordinary laptop CPU is perfectly usable.

**Does Ollama work offline?**
Yes — after the one-time model download. Install and pull your models while online, then everything runs without internet.

**Is my data really private?**
Your prompts stay on your machine when you use Ollama locally — there's no account and nothing is sent to a server. (This applies to local use; if you later connect Open WebUI to a cloud API, that provider's terms apply.)

**How much disk space do models take?**
Roughly 2GB for a 3B model, ~5GB for an 8B model, ~9GB for a 14B model. Check with `ollama list` and delete what you don't use.

**Can I use local models in my own apps?**
Yes — Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible API at `http://localhost:11434/v1`, so most tools and code that talk to OpenAI-style endpoints can point at your local models instead.

title: AI Video (Runway, Pika, Luma): Stop Burning Credits on Warped Faces
description: Your character's face melts at second three — and you just paid for the privilege. Warped faces aren't bad luck; they're the predictable failure mode of every AI video tool. Here's how to stop paying for it.
content:
# AI Video (Runway, Pika, Luma): Stop Burning Credits on Warped Faces

**Your character's face melts at second three — and you just paid for the privilege. Warped faces aren't bad luck; they're the predictable failure mode of every AI video tool. Here's how to stop paying for it.**

---

## What you'll need

- An account on **Runway**, **Pika**, or **Luma** (free tiers work fine for practicing these techniques)
- **One good reference image** of your character: clear, front-facing, well-lit
- A **shot list** written *before* you generate anything — deciding shots at generation time is how credits die

This tutorial covers all three platforms because the techniques are 80% the same. Platform-specific notes are marked where they matter.

---

## First, the honest paragraph: why faces warp

AI video models don't film anything — they hallucinate one frame after another, and each new frame is a guess built on the pixels of the last one. Faces are the worst possible subject for this process: they're the highest-detail region in the frame and the region humans scrutinize most ruthlessly — eyes, teeth, symmetry, skin texture. A tiny error in frame 1 compounds into visible drift by frame 30 and a stranger's face by frame 60. The model has no memory of what your character "really" looks like; it only has the pixels it just invented. That's why warped faces are structural, not a settings mistake — and why the fixes below are about *anchoring identity* rather than tweaking sliders.

---

## Technique 1: Write prompts the model can actually follow

Most warped faces start as bad prompts. Long, ambitious prompts don't give you more control — they give the model more ways to fail.

**The rules:**

1. **One action per shot.** `She turns her head slowly to the left, soft smile` beats `she turns, smiles, waves, and the camera orbits while birds fly past`. Every extra action is another chance for the face to break mid-motion.
2. **Front-load the subject and the single motion.** Put what matters first: the character, then the one movement, then the camera. Style and mood go last.
3. **Use real camera language.** Models respond well to concrete cinematography terms: *slow dolly in, static tripod shot, shallow depth of field, handheld shake, over-the-shoulder.* "Cinematic" alone means nothing — it's a vibe word, not an instruction.
4. **Keep it short.** A tight two-line prompt with one clear action consistently outperforms a paragraph of adjectives. If you can't describe the shot in two sentences, split it into two shots.

**Example:**

> Bloated: `A cinematic ultra-detailed beautiful woman with flowing hair walking through a neon city at night while the camera dramatically sweeps around her and rain begins to fall and she looks up at the sky smiling`
>
> Disciplined: `Medium close-up of a woman with long dark hair, neon-lit street behind her. She slowly looks up and smiles. Static camera, shallow depth of field.`

The second prompt gives the model one face, one motion, and one camera. That's a face it can keep intact.

[SCREENSHOT: side-by-side of a bloated prompt vs. a disciplined prompt in a generation UI]

---

## Technique 2: Anchor identity with reference images

This is the single biggest lever on face quality. Instead of describing your character in words and hoping, you **upload a reference image** and attach it to every generation — giving the model pixels to hold onto instead of a guess.

- **Runway — References.** Runway's Gen-4 reference system lets you upload up to three reference images (character, location, style) that the model holds consistent across shots — no retraining needed.
- **Pika — reference/scene workflows.** Use Pika's scene and frame features with your character image as the reference input, so each generation starts from your character's actual face rather than a text description.
- **Luma — reference-powered generation.** Attach your character image as a reference on generations where identity matters.

**The discipline that makes it work:**

1. **Same reference image for every shot of the character.** Not a similar one — the *same file*. Generate all of a character's shots in one session.
2. **Distinctive costumes and props survive better than subtle facial features.** A red jacket and a specific hairstyle anchor identity far more reliably than cheekbone structure.
3. **Accept 70–80% consistency as success** and plan your edit around the variation: cutaways, reaction shots, and a consistent color grade hide most identity drift.
4. For multi-shot sequences, prefer **image-to-video** (starting from a real frame) over text-to-video whenever a hero character is on screen — text-to-video has no identity anchor at all.

> Feature names and button labels move fast in this space. If a name above has changed in the current UI, the workflow hasn't: same reference image, attached to every shot.

[SCREENSHOT: Runway's References panel with a character image uploaded and attached to a generation]

---

## Technique 3: Chain shots with the last-frame workflow

AI models have short memories — you can't generate a consistent 60-second scene in one go. The professional workaround:

1. Generate **shot 1** (image-to-video, reference attached).
2. Take the **last frame** of shot 1 and use it as the **start image** for shot 2, with the character reference attached again.
3. Repeat.

This "dual image" input — previous shot's ending state plus the identity reference — locks continuity far better than text alone. It also forces you to plan in short shots (5–10 seconds), which is exactly the length where faces survive best. Longer clips don't just cost more credits; they warp more, because more frames means more drift.

---

## Technique 4: The fix-vs-regenerate decision

Every warped clip presents the same question: **fix it or burn another generation?** Decide in the first two seconds of watching the output:

**Regenerate when:**
- The face warps in the **first 1–2 seconds** — the foundation is broken; editing can't save it
- The identity is wrong (wrong person entirely)
- The composition is broken (character half out of frame, extra limbs)

**Fix/edit when:**
- The face is right but a **small glitch** appears later — a flickering hand, a shifting background
- Use the platform's edit tools instead of a full regeneration: region-based editing (Pika's Modify Region), video restyling (Luma's Modify Video), or Runway's editing suite. Touching up one region costs a fraction of a fresh generation.

**And the rule above both:** prototype cheap. Run draft or low-resolution tests first (Luma's Draft Mode exists precisely for this), and only spend full-quality credits on shots that survived the cheap test.

[SCREENSHOT: a generation's credit cost shown on-screen before confirming — always check this number]

---

## Credit math: budget like a producer

Credits are not videos. Every attempt — including failures — burns credits, so **budget 3–5 attempts per keeper shot**, not one. Approximate math per platform (entry paid plans; confirm live numbers before buying):

| Platform | Entry plan | Credits/mo | What that buys (approx) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Runway** | Standard $15/mo ($12 annual) | 625 | ~10 five-second Gen-4.5 clips (60 credits each) — roughly one minute of footage |
| **Pika** | Standard $10/mo ($8 annual) | 700 | ~17 five-second 1080p clips (~40 credits each) |
| **Luma** | Plus $30/mo | 10,000 | ~12 ten-second videos (third-party guideline of ~800 credits each — varies by resolution, model, and retries) |

Three budget rules that follow from the math:

1. **A 60-second video needs ~12 five-second keepers.** At 3–5 attempts each, that's 36–60 generations — on Runway Standard, nearly the entire month. Step up a tier before starting a project, not mid-way.
2. **Entry-plan credits generally don't roll over.** Unused credits expire at renewal on most entry tiers — but that cuts both ways: don't hoard, and don't assume next month bails you out.
3. **Spend your first 20% of credits on cheap tests.** Draft modes and lower resolutions exist to absorb your experiments. Full-quality credits are for keepers.

---

## Common mistakes table

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Regenerating a face that broke in second 1 | Same warp, full price, five times in a row | Kill it fast — fix the prompt/reference, then regenerate once |
| Three actions in one prompt | Model drops or scrambles the middle action; face breaks mid-motion | One action per shot |
| New reference image per shot | Identity drifts between shots | Same reference file, every shot, one session |
| Text-to-video for a hero character | No identity anchor; a different face every time | Image-to-video with a reference attached |
| Generating finals before tests | Paying full price for experiments | Draft/low-res tests first; master only survivors |

chapters.title: What you'll need
chapters.content:
Your character's face melts at second three — and you just paid for the privilege. Warped faces aren't bad luck; they're the predictable failure mode of every AI video tool. Here's how to stop paying for it.

  • An account on Runway, Pika, or Luma (free tiers work fine for practicing these techniques)
  • One good reference image of your character: clear, front-facing, well-lit
  • A shot list written before you generate anything — deciding shots at generation time is how credits die

This tutorial covers all three platforms because the techniques are 80% the same. Platform-specific notes are marked where they matter.

chapters.title: First, the honest paragraph: why faces warp
chapters.content: AI video models don't film anything — they hallucinate one frame after another, and each new frame is a guess built on the pixels of the last one. Faces are the worst possible subject for this process: they're the highest-detail region in the frame and the region humans scrutinize most ruthlessly — eyes, teeth, symmetry, skin texture. A tiny error in frame 1 compounds into visible drift by frame 30 and a stranger's face by frame 60. The model has no memory of what your character "really" looks like; it only has the pixels it just invented. That's why warped faces are structural, not a settings mistake — and why the fixes below are about anchoring identity rather than tweaking sliders.

chapters.title: Technique 1: Write prompts the model can actually follow
chapters.content:
Most warped faces start as bad prompts. Long, ambitious prompts don't give you more control — they give the model more ways to fail.

The rules:

  1. One action per shot. She turns her head slowly to the left, soft smile beats she turns, smiles, waves, and the camera orbits while birds fly past. Every extra action is another chance for the face to break mid-motion.
  2. Front-load the subject and the single motion. Put what matters first: the character, then the one movement, then the camera. Style and mood go last.
  3. Use real camera language. Models respond well to concrete cinematography terms: slow dolly in, static tripod shot, shallow depth of field, handheld shake, over-the-shoulder. "Cinematic" alone means nothing — it's a vibe word, not an instruction.
  4. Keep it short. A tight two-line prompt with one clear action consistently outperforms a paragraph of adjectives. If you can't describe the shot in two sentences, split it into two shots.

Example:

Bloated: A cinematic ultra-detailed beautiful woman with flowing hair walking through a neon city at night while the camera dramatically sweeps around her and rain begins to fall and she looks up at the sky smiling

Disciplined: Medium close-up of a woman with long dark hair, neon-lit street behind her. She slowly looks up and smiles. Static camera, shallow depth of field.

The second prompt gives the model one face, one motion, and one camera. That's a face it can keep intact.

chapters.title: Technique 2: Anchor identity with reference images
chapters.content:
This is the single biggest lever on face quality. Instead of describing your character in words and hoping, you upload a reference image and attach it to every generation — giving the model pixels to hold onto instead of a guess.

  • Runway — References. Runway's Gen-4 reference system lets you upload up to three reference images (character, location, style) that the model holds consistent across shots — no retraining needed.
  • Pika — reference/scene workflows. Use Pika's scene and frame features with your character image as the reference input, so each generation starts from your character's actual face rather than a text description.
  • Luma — reference-powered generation. Attach your character image as a reference on generations where identity matters.

The discipline that makes it work:

  1. Same reference image for every shot of the character. Not a similar one — the same file. Generate all of a character's shots in one session.
  2. Distinctive costumes and props survive better than subtle facial features. A red jacket and a specific hairstyle anchor identity far more reliably than cheekbone structure.
  3. Accept 70–80% consistency as success and plan your edit around the variation: cutaways, reaction shots, and a consistent color grade hide most identity drift.
  4. For multi-shot sequences, prefer image-to-video (starting from a real frame) over text-to-video whenever a hero character is on screen — text-to-video has no identity anchor at all.

Feature names and button labels move fast in this space. If a name above has changed in the current UI, the workflow hasn't: same reference image, attached to every shot.

[SCREENSHOT: Runway's References panel with a character image uploaded and attached to a generation]

chapters.title: Technique 3: Chain shots with the last-frame workflow
chapters.content:
AI models have short memories — you can't generate a consistent 60-second scene in one go. The professional workaround:

  1. Generate shot 1 (image-to-video, reference attached).
  2. Take the last frame of shot 1 and use it as the start image for shot 2, with the character reference attached again.
  3. Repeat.

This "dual image" input — previous shot's ending state plus the identity reference — locks continuity far better than text alone. It also forces you to plan in short shots (5–10 seconds), which is exactly the length where faces survive best. Longer clips don't just cost more credits; they warp more, because more frames means more drift.

chapters.title: Technique 4: The fix-vs-regenerate decision
chapters.content:
Every warped clip presents the same question: fix it or burn another generation? Decide in the first two seconds of watching the output:

Regenerate when:

  • The face warps in the first 1–2 seconds — the foundation is broken; editing can't save it
  • The identity is wrong (wrong person entirely)
  • The composition is broken (character half out of frame, extra limbs)

Fix/edit when:

  • The face is right but a small glitch appears later — a flickering hand, a shifting background
  • Use the platform's edit tools instead of a full regeneration: region-based editing (Pika's Modify Region), video restyling (Luma's Modify Video), or Runway's editing suite. Touching up one region costs a fraction of a fresh generation.

And the rule above both: prototype cheap. Run draft or low-resolution tests first (Luma's Draft Mode exists precisely for this), and only spend full-quality credits on shots that survived the cheap test.

chapters.title: Credit math: budget like a producer
chapters.content:
Credits are not videos. Every attempt — including failures — burns credits, so budget 3–5 attempts per keeper shot, not one. Approximate math per platform (entry paid plans; confirm live numbers before buying):

PlatformEntry planCredits/moWhat that buys (approx)
RunwayStandard $15/mo ($12 annual)625~10 five-second Gen-4.5 clips (60 credits each) — roughly one minute of footage
PikaStandard $10/mo ($8 annual)700~17 five-second 1080p clips (~40 credits each)
LumaPlus $30/mo10,000~12 ten-second videos (third-party guideline of ~800 credits each — varies by resolution, model, and retries)

Three budget rules that follow from the math:

  1. A 60-second video needs ~12 five-second keepers. At 3–5 attempts each, that's 36–60 generations — on Runway Standard, nearly the entire month. Step up a tier before starting a project, not mid-way.
  2. Entry-plan credits generally don't roll over. Unused credits expire at renewal on most entry tiers — but that cuts both ways: don't hoard, and don't assume next month bails you out.
  3. Spend your first 20% of credits on cheap tests. Draft modes and lower resolutions exist to absorb your experiments. Full-quality credits are for keepers.
